Newly hatched Marbled murrelet chicks emerge at a remarkably modest body mass, with neonates typically weighing 32 grams [Wwb = 32 grams] upon first emergence from the egg. This initial wet weight is quite low relative to the species' ultimate adult size, reflecting the altricial-to-semi-precocial developmental strategy common among alcids. The developmental milestones that follow are tightly linked to the species' endothermic physiology; at the typical active body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the nestling phase proceeds rapidly. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at roughly 28 days after hatching [tx = roughly 28 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is typical for a bird of its body size and is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable marine food supply that characterizes the murrelet's coastal breeding habitats along the Pacific Northwest.

Sexual maturation in the Marbled murrelet proceeds along a somewhat extended developmental timeline compared to some other small alcids. Puberty is attained at approximately 84 days after hatching [tp = approximately 84 days after hatching], a milestone representing the onset of gonadal activity and gametogenesis that occurs well before the bird reaches its full adult body mass at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is around 222 grams [Wwi = around 222 grams], a value that represents the asymptotic mass achieved after the completion of somatic growth. The substantial increase in body mass from the 32 gram birth weight to the around 222 gram adult weight reflects a period of rapid post-fledging growth and extensive lipid deposition, necessary for the energetically demanding lifestyle of a pursuit-diving seabird that forages in cold coastal waters. Remarkably, despite reaching sexual competence early, the species defers first reproduction for an extended period, constrained by the need to secure suitable nest sites and build sufficient body condition.

The species exhibits a notably slow pace of life for a bird of its size, with maximum recorded longevity reaching approximately 10365 days [am = approximately 10365 days] under natural conditions at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to over 28 years, is exceptional among alcids of comparable mass and is maintained at a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. First reproduction is deferred considerably relative to the onset of sexual maturity, with the first successful brood typically occurring at around 730 days after hatching [tR = around 730 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This two-year delay between reaching puberty at approximately 84 days and actually initiating breeding reflects the complex social and ecological constraints faced by this species, including the need to secure a suitable nest site in old-growth forest stands, acquire a mate, and build sufficient body condition to support egg production and incubation.

Annual reproductive output in the Marbled murrelet is remarkably constrained, consistent with its extreme longevity and delayed maturity. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a fixed clutch size that is invariant across the species' range and typical of the genus Brachyramphus. At the typical active body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the maximum frequency of nesting attempts is limited to approximately one clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch per year]. This combination of a single-egg clutch and annual breeding frequency means that the maximum annual reproductive output is just a single offspring per year per breeding female. The energetic investment in that single egg is substantial, however, as murrelets produce one of the largest eggs relative to body size among all alcids, representing a significant proportion of the female's own around 222 gram adult body mass.

Post-fledging care in the Marbled murrelet extends well beyond nest departure, with the fledgling remaining dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks while it develops full flight capability and underwater foraging skills. The species demonstrates a remarkable physiological adaptation for diving in cold coastal waters: resting metabolic rates are elevated to support thermoregulation, and the accumulation of lipid reserves during the post-fledging period is critical for winter survival. The seasonal movements of this species are closely tied to prey availability, with individuals traveling substantial distances along the Pacific coast to locate aggregations of small schooling fish and krill. Within the family Alcidae, the Marbled murrelet is exceptional for its reliance on old-growth coniferous forests for nesting, a habitat requirement that creates unique conservation challenges and underscores the strong link between terrestrial and marine ecosystems that defines its life history.
